## Tidy column names

```{r}
library(stringr)

# Standardize names using tidyverse string manipulation
population <- population_raw %>% 
  rename_with(~ .x %>% 
                str_trim() %>%                 # Remove leading/trailing spaces
                str_replace_all("\\s+", "_") %>% # Replace spaces/periods with underscores
                str_replace_all("[\\(\\).,]", "") %>% # Remove punctuation like brackets
                str_to_lower()                 # Convert everything to lowercase
  )

# Verify the changes
names(population)
```

## Outlier check with box plots

Box plots of the standardised (z-scored) quantitative variables let us compare
spread on a single axis and spot extreme values.

```{r eda-boxplots, fig.height=6}
pop_long <- population %>%
  select(all_of(quant_vars)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)))) %>%   # z-scores
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "z")

ggplot(pop_long, aes(x = reorder(variable, z, FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE), y = z)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = pal_main, alpha = 0.6, outlier.colour = "firebrick",
               outlier.alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Box plots of quantitative variables (standardised)",
       subtitle = "Points in red lie beyond 1.5 × IQR",
       x = NULL, y = "z-score")

```

## Dealing with missing values and outliers

**Missing values.** Numeric columns are imputed with the **median**, which is
robust to skew; any missing categorical label is set to `"Unknown"`.

```{r eda-impute}
population <- population %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "Unknown", .x)))

# confirm no missing values remain
sum(is.na(population))
```

**Outliers.** For this dataset the extreme values in the *population* columns
are **genuine** (China and India really are an order of magnitude larger than
most countries), so they are retained for the ranking tasks. For the
*rate-type* variables used later in the correlation study — `density`,
`growth_rate` and `world_population_percentage` — we apply **IQR capping
(winsorising)** so that a handful of extreme territories do not dominate the
correlations. The capped copies are stored in new `*_capped` columns and the
originals are left untouched.

```{r eda-winsor}
cap_iqr <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- diff(q)
  lo <- q[1] - 1.5 * iqr
  hi <- q[2] + 1.5 * iqr
  pmin(pmax(x, lo), hi)
}

rate_vars <- intersect(c("density_per_km2", "growth_rate",
                         "world_population_percentage"), names(population))

population <- population %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(rate_vars), cap_iqr, .names = "{.col}_capped"))

glue::glue("Winsorised (IQR-capped) copies created for: ",
           "{paste(rate_vars, collapse = ', ')}.")
```

# Task 4.3 — New variable: projected 2030 population

The exponential population-growth model is

$$N_t = P\,e^{rt},$$

where $P$ is the present population (end of **2022**), $r$ the growth rate,
$t$ the number of years ahead, and $e \approx 2.71828$. We project to
**2030**, so $t = 2030 - 2022 = 8$.

The raw `growth_rate` column is inspected first, because the dataset may store
it either as an **annual factor** (values near `1.00`), as a **fraction**
(e.g. `0.021`) or as a **percentage** (e.g. `2.1`). The code converts whichever
form is present into a continuous rate $r$.

```{r proj-rate}
# locate the 2022 population column
pop_2022_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "2022")][1]
med_gr <- median(population$growth_rate, na.rm = TRUE)

r_vec <- dplyr::case_when(
  med_gr > 0.5 & med_gr < 1.5 ~ population$growth_rate - 1,  # annual factor
  med_gr >= 1.5               ~ population$growth_rate / 100, # percentage
  TRUE                        ~ population$growth_rate        # already a fraction
)

glue::glue("Median raw growth_rate = {round(med_gr, 4)}  ->  ",
           "interpreted as {ifelse(med_gr > 0.5 & med_gr < 1.5, 'annual factor (r = rate - 1)', ifelse(med_gr >= 1.5, 'percentage (r = rate / 100)', 'fraction (r = rate)'))}.")
```
```{r proj-compute}
t_years <- 2030 - 2022

population <- population %>%
  mutate(
    r = r_vec,
    pop_2022 = .data[[pop_2022_col]],
    projected_2030 = round(pop_2022 * exp(r * t_years))
  )

population %>%
  select(country = matches("country"), continent,
         pop_2022, growth_rate, r, projected_2030) %>%
  arrange(desc(pop_2022)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(caption = "Projected 2030 population (top 10 countries by 2022 population)",
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

# Task 4.4 — Top-10 most populous countries: values and plots

## 4.4.1 Top 10 by 2022 population

```{r top10}
country_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "country")][1]

top10 <- population %>%
  arrange(desc(pop_2022)) %>%
  slice(1:10) %>%
  mutate(country = .data[[country_col]])

top10_names <- top10$country
top10_names
```
     
```{r top10-bar}
ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(country, pop_2022), y = pop_2022)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_main) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())(pop_2022)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale()),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 most populous countries, 2022",
       x = NULL, y = "Population (2022)")
```

## 4.4.2 Population trend 1990–2022 for the top 10

The population dataset reports census snapshots (1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020,
2022). We reshape those columns to long format and plot the trend.

```{r top10-trend}
year_cols <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "^x(19|20)\\d{2}_population$")]
year_co

trend <- top10 %>%
  select(country, all_of(year_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(year_cols), names_to = "year", values_to = "pop") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}"))) %>%
  filter(year >= 1990)

ggplot(trend, aes(year, pop, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(title = "Population trend of the 10 most populous countries, 1990–2022",
       x = "Year", y = "Population", colour = NULL)
```

## 4.4.3 CO~2~ emission trend 1990–2019 for the same countries

```{r co2-prep}
co2 <- co2_raw %>% clean_names()

# The CSV ships a duplicated 2019 column, which readr renames to x2019_34 /
# x2019_35. Match the year anywhere in the name (not an exact x2019) and then
# collapse any duplicate country-year cells by averaging, so 2019 is retained.
co2_year_cols <- names(co2)[str_detect(names(co2), "^x(19|20)\\d{2}")]
co2_country_col <- names(co2)[str_detect(names(co2), "country_name|country$")][1]

co2_long <- co2 %>%
  rename(country = all_of(co2_country_col)) %>%
  select(country, all_of(co2_year_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(co2_year_cols), names_to = "year", values_to = "co2_pc") %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(year, "\\d{4}"))) %>%
  group_by(country, year) %>%
  summarise(co2_pc = mean(co2_pc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(co2_pc = ifelse(is.nan(co2_pc), NA_real_, co2_pc))

# match the top-10 country names (handles minor naming differences)
name_fix <- c("United States" = "United States",
              "Russia" = "Russian Federation",
              "Egypt" = "Egypt, Arab Rep.")
top10_co2_names <- recode(top10_names, !!!name_fix)

co2_top10 <- co2_long %>%
  filter(country %in% c(top10_names, top10_co2_names),
         year >= 1990, year <= 2019)
```

```{r co2-trend}
ggplot(co2_top10, aes(year, co2_pc, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(title = "CO2 emission trend of the 10 most populous countries, 1990–2019",
       subtitle = "Metric tons per capita",
       x = "Year", y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita)", colour = NULL)
```

# Task 4.5 — Correlation analysis

## 4.5.1 Correlations within the population dataset

Correlations between **Area**, **Density**, **Growth rate** and **World
population percentage** (using the IQR-capped rate variables), shown both as a
numeric matrix and as a heatmap.

```{r corr-pop}
area_col <- names(population)[str_detect(names(population), "area")][1]

corr_df <- population %>%
  transmute(
    Area        = .data[[area_col]],
    Density     = density_per_km2_capped,
    Growth_rate = growth_rate_capped,
    World_pct   = world_population_percentage_capped
  )

corr_mat <- cor(corr_df, use = "complete.obs")
round(corr_mat, 3) %>% kable(caption = "Correlation matrix (population variables)")
```

```{r corr-heatmap}
corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         addCoef.col = "black", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
         col = colorRampPalette(c("#D73027", "white", "#2C7FB8"))(200),
         mar = c(0, 0, 1, 0), title = "Correlation heatmap: population variables")
```

## 4.5.2 Population vs CO~2~ emissions (merged data)

The two datasets are merged on country name; we then keep **2022 population**
and **2019 CO~2~ emissions** and study the relationship with a scatter plot,
correlation coefficients and a simple linear regression.

```{r merge}
co2_2019 <- co2_long %>%
  filter(year == 2019) %>%
  select(country, co2_2019 = co2_pc)

pop_small <- population %>%
  transmute(country = .data[[country_col]],
            continent,
            pop_2022,
            projected_2030)

# normalise a few well-known name mismatches before joining
norm_name <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_replace_all("United States of America", "United States") %>%
    str_replace_all("Russian Federation", "Russia") %>%
    str_replace_all("Egypt, Arab Rep.", "Egypt") %>%
    str_replace_all("Iran, Islamic Rep.", "Iran") %>%
    str_replace_all("Korea, Rep.", "South Korea") %>%
    str_trim()
}

merged <- pop_small %>%
  mutate(country = norm_name(country)) %>%
  inner_join(co2_2019 %>% mutate(country = norm_name(country)), by = "country") %>%
  filter(!is.na(co2_2019), !is.na(pop_2022))

glue::glue("Countries successfully matched across both datasets: {nrow(merged)}")
```

```{r merge-scatter}
ggplot(merged, aes(pop_2022, co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, colour = pal_main) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(title = "Population (2022) vs CO2 emissions (2019)",
       subtitle = "Log scale on population; per-capita emissions",
       x = "Population 2022 (log scale)",
       y = "CO2 (metric tons per capita, 2019)")
```

```{r merge-corr}
pear <- cor(merged$pop_2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "pearson")
spear <- cor(merged$pop_2022, merged$co2_2019, method = "spearman")
pear_log <- cor(log10(merged$pop_2022), merged$co2_2019, method = "pearson")

tibble(
  Measure = c("Pearson (raw)", "Spearman (rank)", "Pearson (log population)"),
  Value   = round(c(pear, spear, pear_log), 3)
) %>% kable(caption = "Association between 2022 population and 2019 CO2 per capita")

lm_fit <- lm(co2_2019 ~ log10(pop_2022), data = merged)
summary(lm_fit)
```

# Task 4.6 — Comparing CO~2~ emissions across continents

Using the merged data we sum the **2019 per-capita CO~2~ emissions** within each
continent and compare them graphically.

```{r continent}
cont_co2 <- merged %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(total_co2_2019 = sum(co2_2019, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_countries = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(total_co2_2019))

cont_co2 %>% kable(caption = "Total 2019 CO2 (metric tons per capita) by continent",
                   digits = 2)
```

```{r continent-plot}
ggplot(cont_co2, aes(x = reorder(continent, total_co2_2019), y = total_co2_2019)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal_main) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(total_co2_2019, 1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Total 2019 CO2 emissions by continent",
       subtitle = "Sum of per-capita values across matched countries",
       x = NULL, y = "Total CO2 (metric tons per capita)")
```

**Answers to the questions (computed from the data):**

```{r continent-answers, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
r1 <- cont_co2 %>% slice(1)
r3 <- cont_co2 %>% slice(3)
rl <- cont_co2 %>% slice(n())

cat(sprintf("1. **Highest 2019 CO2 emission:** %s (total %.2f metric tons per capita).\n\n",
            r1$continent, r1$total_co2_2019))
cat(sprintf("2. **Third-ranked continent:** %s, with a total of %.2f metric tons per capita.\n\n",
            r3$continent, r3$total_co2_2019))
cat(sprintf("3. **Lowest-ranked continent:** %s, with a total of %.2f metric tons per capita.\n\n",
            rl$continent, rl$total_co2_2019))
```

```{r write-summary, include=FALSE}
# Export the headline numbers so the LaTeX report can quote them exactly.
summary_lines <- c(
  sprintf("rows_pop=%d", nrow(population)),
  sprintf("cols_pop=%d", ncol(population_raw)),
  sprintf("matched_countries=%d", nrow(merged)),
  sprintf("pearson_raw=%.3f", pear),
  sprintf("spearman=%.3f", spear),
  sprintf("pearson_log=%.3f", pear_log),
  sprintf("lm_slope=%.3f", coef(lm_fit)[2]),
  sprintf("lm_r2=%.3f", summary(lm_fit)$r.squared),
  sprintf("top_continent=%s|%.2f", r1$continent, r1$total_co2_2019),
  sprintf("third_continent=%s|%.2f", r3$continent, r3$total_co2_2019),
  sprintf("last_continent=%s|%.2f", rl$continent, rl$total_co2_2019),
  sprintf("top10=%s", paste(top10_names, collapse = "; "))
)
writeLines(summary_lines, file.path(getwd(), "results_summary.txt"))
```

---

# Conclusion

The analysis cleaned and prepared the World Population Dataset, projected each
country's population to 2030 with the exponential growth model, identified and
visualised the ten most populous countries and their population and CO~2~
trends, and quantified the link between population and per-capita emissions
through correlation and regression. The continent comparison summarises where
per-capita emissions concentrate. Full narrative discussion, limitations and
recommendations are provided in the accompanying LaTeX report.

check <- function(x) {
  if(is.na(x)) {
    print(paste(x, " is a missing value"))
  }
  if(x > 0) {
    print(paste(x, " is greater than zero"))
  } else {
    print(paste(x, " is equal or less than zero"))
  }
}
